Richard Sutton's The Bitter Lesson is one of the best articulations of why huge chunks of research are destined to be irrelevant as a consequence of scale. This makes people super mad, but also seems like a real phenomenon.

There are endless debates in policy forums about how important it is to focus on symbolic systems as well as deep learning systems. It's frequently unclear what people mean by symbolic and there aren't many benchmarks (any?) where symbolic systems show up. Dark matter.

It is extremely bad that most of the people with significant political power in the US and other govs are 50+. They do not conceptualize this stuff the same way younger people do, and therefore don't recognize as legitimate a bunch of fears and opportunities.

Policy is a gigantic random number generator - some random event might trigger some politician to have a deep opinion about an aspect of AI, after which they don't update further. This can brick long-term projects randomly (very relaxing).

To get stuff done in policy you have to be wildly specific. CERN for AI? Cute idea. Now tell me about precise funding mechanisms, agency ownership, plan for funding over long-term. If you don't do the details, you don't get stuff done.

Most policy forums involve people giving canned statements of their positions, and everyone thanks eachother for giving their positions, then you agree it was good to have a diverse set of perspectives, then the event ends. Huge waste of everyone's time.

Correspondingly, one of the ways to be least effective in policy is to base your position around qualitative interpretations of the domain, and to mostly use rhetoric to make your points - this makes people switch off.

Policy is permissionless - companies drill employees to not talk to policymakers and only let those talks happen through gov affairs teams and choreographed meetings. This isn't a law, it's just brainwashing. Engineers should talk directly to policy people.

Discussions about AGI tend to be pointless as no one has a precise definition of AGI, and most people have radically different definitions. In many ways, AGI feels more like a shibboleth used to understand if someone is in- or out-group wrt some issues.

Most technologist feel like they can do anything wrt AI because governments (in West) have shown pretty much zero interest in regulating AI, beyond punishing infractions in a small number of products. Many orgs do skeezy shit under the radar and gamble no one will notice.

@HeidyKhlaaf I just mean that in lots of multi-stakeholder policy meetings, there's a general prior that it's not possible to build general or intelligent things. This is strange as I work with a bunch of people who think you can do this.

It's likely that companies are one of the most effective ways to build decent AI systems - companies have money, can move quickly, and have fewer stakeholders than governments. This is a societal failing and many problems in AI deployment stem from this basic fact.

@riptari Extremely worried about rapid advance of AI capabilities unlocking dangerous things (e.g, models that suddenly know how to make extremely good pathogens), but the dangerous things are unlocked as a byproduct of broader development, so go unnoticed till someone finds them.

@riptari Extremely worried about intersection of malware and AI tools (economic incentives will drive utilization which will destroy huge amounts of digital infrastructure - we'll look back at the current ransomware era as much easier and cheaper to deal with).

Lots of the seemingly most robust solutions for reducing AI risk require the following things to happen: full information sharing on capabilities between US and China and full monitoring of software being run on all computers everywhere all the time. Pretty hard to do!

AI policy is anti-democratic for the same reasons as large-scale AI being anti-democratic - companies have money, so they can build teams to turn up at meetings all the time and slowly move the overton window. It's hard to do this if it's not your dayjob.

People wildly underestimate how much influence individuals can have in policy. I've had a decent amount of impact by just turning up and working on the same core issues (measurement and monitoring) for multiple years. This is fun, but also scares the shit out of me.

AI really is going to change the world. Things are going to get 100-1000X cheaper and more efficient. This is mostly great. However, historically, when you make stuff 100X-1000X cheaper, you upend the geopolitical order. This time probably won't be different.

It's functionally impossible to talk about the weird (and legitimate) problems of AI alignment in public/broad forums (e.g, this twitter thread). It is like signing up to be pelted with rotten vegetables, or called a bigot. This makes it hard to discuss these issues in public.

Some people who work on frontier AI policy think a legitimate goal of AI policy should be to ensure governments (especially US government) has almost no understanding of rate of progress at the frontier, thinking it safer for companies to rambo this solo (I disagree with this).

Sometimes, bigtech companies seem to go completely batshit about some AI policy issue, and 90% of the time it's because some internal group has figured out a way to run an internal successful political campaign and the resulting policy moves are about hiring retention.

Some companies deliberately keep their AI policy teams AWAY from engineers. I regularly get emails from engineers at $bigtech asking me to INTRO THEM to their own policy teams, or give them advice on how to raise policy issues with them.

Like 95% of the immediate problems of AI policy are just "who has power under capitalism", and you literally can't do anything about it. AI costs money. Companies have money. Therefore companies build AI. Most talk about democratization is PR-friendly bullshit that ignores this.

The default outcome of current AI policy trends in the West is we all get to live in Libertarian Snowcrash wonderland where a small number of companies rewire the world. Everyone can see this train coming along and can't work out how to stop it.

The notion of building 'general' and 'intelligent' things is broadly frowned on in most AI policy meetings. Many people have a prior that it's impossible for any machine learning-based system to be actually smart. These people also don't update in response to progress.

Many of the immediate problems of AI (e.g, bias) are so widely talked about because they're at least somewhat tractable (you can make measures, you can assess, you can audit). Many of the longterm problems aren't discussed because no one has a clue what to do about them.

A surprisingly large amount of AI policy is illegible, because mostly the PR-friendly stuff gets published, and many of the smartest people working in AI policy circulate all their stuff privately (this is a weird dynamic and probably a quirk/departure from norm)

Most technical people think policy can't matter for AI, because of the aforementioned unfathomably-behind nature of most governments. A surprisingly large % of people who think this also think this isn't a problem.

Lots of AI policy teams are disempowered because they have no direct technical execution ability - they need to internally horse-trade to get anything done, so they aren't able to do much original research, and mostly rebrand existing projects.

Many of the problems in AI policy stem from the fact that economy-of-scale capitalism is, by nature, anti-democratic, and capex-intensive AI is therefore anti-democratic. No one really wants to admit this. It's awkward to bring it up at parties (I am not fun at parties).

Many AI policy teams in industry are constructed as basic the second line of brand defense after the public relations team. A huge % of policy work is based around reacting to perceived optics problems, rather than real problems.

The real danger in Western AI policy isn't that AI is doing bad stuff, it's that governments are so unfathomably behind the frontier that they have no notion of _how_ to regulate, and it's unclear if they _can_
There is not some secret team working for a government in the West building incredibly large-scale general models. There are teams doing applied work in intelligence.
China has a much more well-developed AI policy approach than that in Europe and the United States. China is actually surprisingly good at regulating things around, say, synthetic media.

Another big moment was when I was able to cook a can of soup for myself, and I was very grateful to have been able to prepare myself a meal. Later, when I was able to walk with a cane, my partner and I went and looked at ducks by Lake Merrit and it was very joyful.

Most of all I learned the value of kindness. My partner kept me fed and watched over me as I slowly relearned to walk. One day I fell over and couldn't get up for 3 hours and she came and 'camped' with me in the hall of our apartment till I could move again.

Chronic pain makes you really stupid. I basically couldn't think for 2-3 weeks as I was mostly directing my mental attention to my body, and constantly watching myself for signs of spasms. All I could really do was rest and sleep and take medicine and sometimes watch TV.

I had back spasms that were so bad they'd physically bounce me out of bed. I became acutely paranoid about sharp things in my room as there was a real risk I'd hit my head on them when spasming. The spasms were easily a 10 on the 0-10 pain scale.

Being genuinely disabled is really frightening. I couldn't feed myself for the first few days. Any time I needed to go to bathroom I had to do it predominantly using upper body strength. Sometimes I'd fall over and not be able to get up for hours.

Therefore, AI may also be a force that creates a dragging influence on cultural evolution, as a tiny set of actors make these models, and each time they emit them, they release artefacts that emphasize a frozen aspect of culture. Something to think about.

At a high level, AI holds the possibility of trapping us in a specific kind of amber. We are injecting culture with systems that repeat and amplify the memes and ideologies they were created within, and these systems may ultimately be more scalable than human production.

Many people have written about how this can create certain kinds of harms and benefits. I suspect the more pernicious effect is how AI creates systems that repeat and re-emphasize cultural snapshots cast in amber at the moment the model was trained on a specific dataset.

One of the amazing and also frightening things about AI is how it magnifies and repeats the 'culture' that it is trained on, where culture is a bunch of implicitly ideological choices on the part of the people that create the underlying datasets.

@utopiah I think it's broadly true. We have technologies to have much cleaner energy, great and affordable housing, incredible education for all, total elimination of hunger, easy access to voting for all, etc. But none of these things really happen. That's because of incentives

@ElliottChMiller Probably need to write a longer essay, but a lot of what makes life good is aspects of life that are illegible to the state/other entities. My fear is a lot of AI stuff is going to render the illegible legible, for the purpose of making money. This will mostly be unpleasant

@scottlegrand There's a set of things these systems can do, and a set of things they can't do, and the trend is the capabilities are expanding over time. I'm not tweeting the above to be boosterish, just to note we're in an era where AI systems are being widely deployed for good and bad

The thing about AI is every positive use is accompanied with a plausible negative use. The incentive structures of the world probably incentivize more negative uses than positive ones. Because AI is dependent on capital, most AI is going to try to 'extract value' globally.

AI systems are also dramatically improving the ability for states to surveil their citizens, are learning to hack (and defend) in domain of computer security, are creating reliable killer-drones, are faking images, and are making it much easier to produce cheap disinformation.

AI systems are solving math olympiad problems, becoming competitive with humans in programming competitions, speeding up science via improved protein structure predictions, writing poems and fiction that people enjoy, and revolutionizing our ability to monitor a changing climate

@_TimOBrien A lot of this paper argues government needs to build own direct capacity to measure/monitor itself, rather than being entirely dependent on outsourcing. Part of why it's so critical gov invest in this is to develop its own capacity so it doesn't get fleeced. Agree!

Finally, much of this work is built on examples generated by others. One of the best examples is Gender Shades by Buolamwini et al - this showed that by measuring a deployed AI system you can identify real harm. That's exactly what we should be doing systematically at scale.

I'm going to spend the next few months trying to get various govs to implement measuring and monitoring schemes. I'd also be excited to debate this idea - do you massively disagree with it? If so, reach out and let me know! Let's get into it!

This paper lays out some of the 'why' for the need to measure and monitor AI, and also has some ideas for how to operationalize these ideas. If you'd like to talk to @jesswhittles  and I about it, please drop me a DM or an email at jack@jack-clark.net

The longer the information disparities go on, the more the private sector is incentivized to produce information that steers governments towards the outcomes it'd like, and the more dependent government becomes on the private sector - that's a very fragile way to build a society https://t.co/wOuSEkw744

I've spent the last few years trying to prototype ways for governments to gather better information about AI (see: @indexingAI). I did this because there's a dangerous information asymmetry about AI in the world - private sector has lots, public sector has little

Why's information about AI important? It tells us about where the technology is heading, where it has weaknesses, and where it may be deployed in the future. All of this is useful stuff for governments to know

Our proposal is pretty simple - governments should monitor and measure the AI ecosystem, both in terms of research and in terms of deployment. Why? This creates information about AI progress (and failures) for the public

Also, to be agonizingly clear, I haven't been the first person to 'discover' this, I more mean I've discovered some surprising (to me) links between journaling and my own mental health and happiness. : )
@kathytpham That's a wonderful thing to hear! I hope you can find time during your very busy schedule to (and I hope you're well)

@NicoleHemsoth Yes, good observation! I did have fitbit for a bit (and now just use Google fit). I think the update I've noticed (realized this in 2020/2021) is that journaling has had quite a meaningful impact on my life, way above any physical habits I've done/got.

9. The modern world wants us to expose/sell/propagate every part of ourself. Having private journals has felt important to counterbalance this. My true self is unbranded and unmonetized, joyfully. The journals are an engine for mental reflection/maintenance. FIN/Happy friday!

8. Intriguingly, the routine of journaling has trained my brain to 'optimize for novelty', because I find journaling more interesting when I have novel stuff to write about. This has caused me to have more intrinsic motivation to put myself in novel situations, which I love.

7. Journaling has helped me get out of pathological spirals - if you read the past two weeks of your diary and see you've turned down every social commitment, that can be a real wake up call. Ditto with saying 'yes' to every work commitment and seeing stress it causes.

6. By journaling, I both reduce the emotional labor others need to invest in me, and I'm better able to spot cases where I should thank or acknowledge acts of kindness others have done for me. This has been especially helpful in my marriage.

5. The act of reflection helps you spot things about yourself that you may not have realized otherwise. I've had emotional and intellectual breakthroughs that have come through writing about myself, to myself, and for myself. There's something very raw and freeing about this.

4. Journals let you 'see yourself'. It's very hard to understand how you as a person behave if you aren't logging it. If you log it, it's easier to see when you're being an asshole, being unfair, or otherwise messing up. You can also tell when you're deluding yourself.

3. By teaching myself to frequently journal, I've meaningfully changed how I approach socializing. Put simply, journaling taught me that denying myself social opportunities for some kind of 'work' is a reliable prelude to my mood dipping and/or depression.

2. By journaling, I've developed much better intuitions /visibility about my natural baselines. What does baseline happy Jack look like? What are symptoms I might be sad? What are symptoms that there's something I myself am unsure about? What hobbies do I actually like?

1. The years when I have barely journaled have correlated to years when I've been depressed and/or unsatisfied with my life in some deep way. I can 'see' myself about to change my life just by looking at the length of journals - once lengths start going up, change is coming.

@Sivasoumitri Hiya, thanks for the kind words. I think there are some things that are actually pretty hard to cure. For instance, I have some physical stuff that relates to how my skeleton is shaped, which is actually extraordinarily hard to deal with.

I have an occasional (thankfully) physical ailment which brings all of this into focus: your money, titles, and audience aren't very useful if your body doesn't work. They can't help you. But the stuff in your own head can, and it's all you've actually got when the stakes rise.

The bigger part of this is that: no one can take this stuff away from you. You can lose titles and money and your audience(s). But it's very hard to lose a palace of ideas you've been building in your own brain for decades. These things are what strength derives from.

Of course it'd be nice to be rich, or a famous artist, or have some big title. But I like walking through the streets with a cane, body half-broken, thinking about stories about alien technology inspired by knots I see in trees, or weeds rising up through pavement cracks.

Contemporary society wants you to optimize for a certain kind of tangible success, like money or significant viewership/readership or having certain fancy titles. Personally, I'm more interested in intangible success - stuff where you can lose everything and it's in your head.

I could keep going and talk about this with pretty much every tech company. As we head into the 2020s, companies are going to compete against how accurately they can simulate and predict culture and cultural production.

When TikTok has a good quarter, its because it has created a better algorithmic underlay which curates the cultural/imaginative landscape of each TikTok instance on a per-user basis, rewarding Bytedance for better autonomously simulating what it thinks is subjectively compelling

When YouTube has a good quarter, it's usually because it has changed underlying behavior of its users to create new ones and increase dedication of existing ones. Most of this relies on YouTube making increasingly compelling recommendations to people on an individual basis.

When Snapchat has a good quarter because it has driven more advertizer interactions via a successful filter, that's more than advertizing - its Snapchat being rewarded for getting inside people's minds and providing them the tools to express their own imagination.

Modern technology companies are increasingly battling for not just consumer attention, but the environments in which attention is shaped - Netflix and Fortnite and Facebook are all battling for a limited amount of imaginative real estate in the heads of most people worldwide

If you want to make a real difference in the world, I I think you need to be idiosyncratic about what you do, which means you need to be willing to be weird yourself. Meaningful success mostly correlates to people who show up, day after day, doing something very weird.
So I think it's a good trade - you're going to lose out on some of the success tchotchkes of contemporary life, but you're going to gain in your own idiosyncratic approach to things.

This approach has drawbacks - it doesn't optimize for typical success, or developing fungible skills. But it does create purpose - if you work on stuff for yourself, you're putting yourself on the line, and not an imagery archetype of a successful person. Real stakes.

The personal challenges of my life have been about trying to spend more time doing the things that feel true to me, and less time doing things that I don't believe in. This has also generally correlated to my happiness and the vibrancy of my inner mental world.

You can convince yourself to do things that the world wants you to do rather than what you want to do, but at some point you'll break mental composure and you'll see the joke, which will diminish the quality of your work. You'll also be unhappy.

If you do things for yourself, then you'll keep doing them forever. If you do things because the world says they're what success comes from, then you'll continually assess your skill at them against some goal&benchmark you don't believe in.

Here's a thread about doing things for yourself vs doing things the world thinks you should do. As I've got older, I've noticed that the more time I spend on the things that make sense to me, the more stable and fulfilled I am.

How does this relate to COVD? I think COVID is going to drive interest in a few quite specific vision-based surveillance techs. I think this will create new markets that some countries will subsequently take advantage of. The long term implications of this shift are meaningful.

What kinds of choices do we have about how this unfolds? How can we better guide different states to different outcomes? And how will evolution of technologies that support faster OODA loops, like AI, influence geopolitics here? Trying to do some thinking around this!

I think the long-term implications of this stuff are pretty difficult for people that like democracies, individual sovereignty, and general notions of freedom. There's going to be a significant economic and security-led pressure for states to digitize&analyze everything.

We'll also find some states will adopt surveillance technologies to massively increase the speed of their OODA loops. China does this a ton already with civil-military integration of surveillance tech. But other states are exploring this stuff as well - UK, Taiwan, Singapore, etc

What does this mean? We'll start to look at states in terms of ability to rapidly understand stuff happening around them, analyze that information, and make policy in response (see: various different responses to COVID usually being function of testing/measurement).

Playing around with notion that we'll evaluate 21st century geopolitics through lens of 'information empires'. It's going to be increasingly apparent that AI-driven OODA loops (https://t.co/AQI9TJ00pk) are going to define competitive dynamics in many areas of life.

These 'information architectures' are important because they have significant economic impacts. They're analogous to the brain-nerve relay systems in our bodies that set a ceiling on how fast we can observe and respond to things. And they're constantly changing!

It's not superficially obvious, but all around us companies like @stripe @Google @amazon @Facebook @AlibabaB2B @TencentGlobal @Microsoft etc are building the tools to let them operate at fundamentally different speeds relative to the rest of the world.

Large companies should employ "system historians" who track and document changes in baroque infrastructures over time. What battles has Google fought over memory allocation during its lifetime? What scheduling systems has Amazon built, refined, retired, and iterated on?

text: @qhardy @mer__edith Maybe. @mer__edith And you can't really put the genie back in the bottle - you can't tell your employees you're "just a company" after doing this for years. People justifiably want you to be more like a state with clear accountability and responsiveness to them.

@mer__edith So if you spend years getting all of your employees aligned around some large social mission and political ethos, you shouldn't be surprised when employees want to push you to have governance and accountability like democratic institutions.

@mer__edith Maybe it's just too compressed for Twitter stuff. Mostly, I think a lot of this is that companies spent years trying to tell their employees they were all one big political entity, and now the chickens are coming home to roost.

@pcihon I also think that companies have spent years telling people that they have certain values and that if you work there you are part of a community/family. It's therefore natural to lobby your company like you would a politician, and natural to run campaigns within it.

@pcihon Yes, I agree with this! I think there are meaningful perception things here - a lot of people don't model the protections afforded to them by government, but do see the harms that government actions create. Additionally, companies try to make employees feel like co = country
The tech worker movement, if you zoom out enough, looks like citizens of various nation states lobbying their various governments to not ally with another country (the US government).

text: @mgubrud I'm interested in having this stuff done for civil purposes and not for secret reports (not that there's anything wrong with that - there's just a lot of it already). I'm not claiming novelty here, I'm mostly advocating for us to fund and do this systematically at societal scale
